analysis.one_liner: Exempts tribal businesses and institutions on tribal lands from federal rules protecting union rights and collective bargaining.
analysis.headline: The bill had 10 Senate sponsors, was referred to the Senate Indian Affairs Committee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that Indian tribes and any business, hospital, school, or other institution owned by a tribe and located on tribal land are treated like state and local governments — which are already outside the National Labor Relations Act. In practice, workers at tribal casinos, hotels, clinics, and other tribal enterprises, including non-tribal members, would no longer have the right to form unions, bargain collectively, or file unfair-labor-practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board. Supporters frame this as tribal self-governance; critics note it removes protections from employees of large commercial businesses without requiring any tribal replacement.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments and tribally owned enterprises — especially casinos, resorts, healthcare facilities, and schools on tribal land — would be freed from National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction, union organizing drives, collective bargaining obligations, and unfair-labor-practice litigation. Supporters say this restores tribal sovereignty by putting tribes in the same position as states and cities, which are exempt from the Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal governments and tribally owned enterprises

how_it_helps.text: Adds Indian tribes, and any enterprise or institution owned and operated by a tribe and located on its lands, to the National Labor Relations Act's definition of 'employer' exclusions, removing them from the Act's coverage.

The Act currently requires covered employers to allow employees to form unions, bargain collectively, and refrain from unfair labor practices; the bill would end those requirements for tribal employers on tribal land.

Defines 'Indian lands' broadly to include all reservation lands, trust and restricted-fee lands, and former reservation boundaries in Oklahoma, so the exemption would cover a wide swath of tribally operated businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at tribally owned businesses on tribal land — including tribal members and non-Indian employees alike — would lose federally guaranteed rights to organize, bargain collectively, and appeal to the National Labor Relations Board, with no requirement that tribes enact their own labor laws in exchange. Unions would also lose jurisdiction over these workplaces.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers at tribally owned businesses on tribal land

drawbacks.text: Tribal enterprises are often large commercial businesses — casinos, hotels, and healthcare systems — that employ many non-tribal members; the bill would strip these workers of federal organizing and bargaining rights while imposing no obligation on tribes to protect those rights under tribal law.
The exemption would create a labor-law imbalance between tribal and non-tribal competitors in gaming and hospitality, since non-tribal casinos and hotels would remain covered by the Act.
The bill defines covered lands to include former Oklahoma reservation boundaries, extending the exemption well beyond present-day reservation trust land.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The sovereignty argument is genuine: states, cities, and counties are already exempt from the Act, and tribes are the other main governments in the country. But the bill goes beyond tribal government functions to cover any tribally owned commercial enterprise, and it offers workers nothing in return — no requirement that tribes pass their own labor protections before taking the exemption. For the many non-tribal members employed by tribal casinos and health systems, the bill is a straight loss of workplace rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Indian Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jerry Moran introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, joined by nine Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Indian Affairs on the day it was introduced.
No further action — no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor debate — was ever recorded, and the bill expired at the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers at tribally owned businesses keep their federal organizing and bargaining rights, and unions keep jurisdiction over tribal enterprises, because the exemption never advanced. Tribal governments and tribal businesses did not get the labor-law carve-out they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers on tribal lands and their unions

for.name: Jerry Moran
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led 9 Republican Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 9 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Senate Democrat did.

against.name: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 initial sponsors were Republicans, and the 9 cosponsors were all Senate Republicans, with no Democratic support in the record; the bill died in a committee without any recorded vote.

industries.industry: Tribal enterprises (casinos, resorts, tribally operated healthcare and schools)
industries.note: The bill would exempt these employers from National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction, union elections, and unfair-labor-practice liability, lowering their labor-law exposure and costs. That gain comes directly out of workers' federally protected organizing and bargaining rights, and would give tribal gaming and hospitality businesses a cost position their non-tribal competitors do not have.
Unions would lose the ability to organize and represent employees at hundreds of tribally owned workplaces on tribal land. The bill's failure preserved their jurisdiction there.

If tribal competitors were exempted from federal labor law, non-tribal casinos and hotels would face a playing field tilted against them on labor costs. The bill died, so the imbalance never took effect.
